THE
BUSHMEN

Every tale leaves a scar.

Written by Jay Green  ·  J.H. Calder

A new Green Beret joins his team in Afghanistan and is drawn into the violent, absurd, and deeply human world of Special Forces combat — where men become legends, and every tale leaves a scar.

Watch the Reel Request Materials

"Men, Special Forces is a mistress. Your wives will envy her because she will have your hearts. Your wives will be jealous of her because of the power to pull you away. This mistress will show you things never before seen and experience things never before felt. She will love you, but only a little, seducing you to want more, give more, die for her. She will take you away from the ones you love, and you will hate her for it, but leave her you never will, but if you must, you will miss her, for she has a part of you that will never be returned intact.

And in the end, she will leave you for a younger man."

James R. WardOffice of Strategic Services (OSS)

The Series

Not the Myth.
The Truth.

For twenty years, every portrayal of Special Forces on screen has been sanitized. Hero-worshipped. Politicized. The Bushmen is the corrective — built on nine combat deployments of lived experience, told with the brutal honesty the subject demands.

Jason Green — 36D1 SF Medic — moves across three ODAs across two deployment cycles, 2013–2015. Each team is a distinct world. Each mission leaves a mark.

"Generation Kill meets The Bear — unsanitized military realism, intimate character drama, dark humor, and the emotional cost of brotherhood."

Jason A. Green  ·  ODA 3336  ·  Afghanistan, 2013–2015

The Truth on Tape

Three ODAs.
One Medic.

The chaos, the boredom, the violence, the laughter, the grief — and the brotherhood that makes survival possible. This is not propaganda. This is not politics. This is the men.

Episode 8: he is shot in the head. The visual grammar fractures with him. Episodes 9–13 are not recovery. They are reckoning.

Every episode ends with an Every Time I Die track. Music is POV — never omniscient.

Brutal Authenticity

Objective camera. No score during contact. The truth of what it actually looks like.

Dark Humor

Gallows humor as survival mechanism. The absurdity is real. So is the laughter.

Intimate Character

Seven men on a team. You know every one of them before the first shot is fired.

Emotional Cost

What goes downrange stays downrange. What comes home is a different problem.

Season One
S01

2013–2015 Afghanistan

Thirteen episodes. Two deployment cycles. The season opens with a green-on-blue attack at VSO Jalrez — objective camera, no score, just the truth — and ends with Jason on a HLZ at Bagram, coming home. Jason moves across ODA 3336 ("Knucks & Chucks"), 3335 ("Necessary Evil"), and 3334 ("Death Machine MC") — the connective tissue of three very different worlds.

J.H. Calder  ·  ODA 3336  ·  Afghanistan

Writer / Director / Showrunner

Jason A. Green

Writing as J.H. Calder

I served nine combat deployments as a Special Forces medic. I've carried men off the battlefield, held their hands while they died, laughed with them around burn barrels. For years, every portrayal of Special Forces on screen felt wrong — sanitized, hero-worshipped, politicized. I never saw my team. I never saw the truth.

My wife Lindsey is a combat veteran and former medic. She survived an IED blast that killed everyone else in her vehicle. Beat cancer. She is the emotional spine of this series. I'm not interested in propaganda or politics. I'm interested in the men I served with — their stories, their laughter, their pain, their ghosts.
